v.why: Under standard parameterization the maximal stable learning rate shrinks with width, so raising it hurts wide nets more.
At tiny learning rates training is step-limited and wider layers reduce loss faster per step, so width substitutes for missing step size.
Large batches mean few, low-noise updates, so a larger step compensates for the step-count bottleneck.
The L2 term is divided by the minibatch size, so small batches multiply the effective penalty and extra alpha over-regularizes them far more.
Strong L2 shrinkage compounds multiplicatively through stacked layers, collapsing signal in deeper nets.
When narrow layers are the capacity bottleneck, an extra layer supplies capacity by another route.
Shallow nets have better-conditioned loss surfaces that tolerate larger Adam steps, so raising the learning rate mostly speeds fitting.
Large batches give few updates in 243 epochs, leaving an added layer undertrained.
With few updates from large batches, wider layers fit faster per step and substitute for the missing optimization steps.
Depth only pays off in a workable optimizer regime; low learning rates leave extra layers untrained and high ones destabilize them.

Two hypotheses are dropped because their condition is the edited parameter's own band: alpha↑ when alpha is high, and learning_rate_init↑ when learning_rate_init is high. None of the rest simply switch off the edited component.

From the remaining 18, I kept 10 that each use a different ordered pair of edited and condition parameter. I preferred ones where an informed expert could reasonably bet either way. For example, Adam's per-parameter scaling makes width–learning-rate effects uncertain. It is also unclear whether alpha in this benchmark is actually divided by batch size. Three of the picks (learning rate, depth and width under large batches) share the "few updates per run" idea, but each edits a different parameter.
